summary:
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands is a Union Territory of India and stands under India's national framework for transgender recognition and protection. No territory-specific trans law, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file, so a visitor to the islands is assessed against the national position, which changed materially in March 2026.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. Protests were held in Mumbai on the day of passage. The bill amends the 2019 law and removes the self-identification route to legal recognition that had been affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014.

Recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, with recognition in practice narrowed to male and female categories plus those traditional identities. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Critics warn the narrower definition excludes self-identifying gender-fluid and non-binary people; rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking.

The amended law mandates medical certification, including medical-board and district-authority certification for gender-affirming surgery, and adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring people to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns these offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment's recognition scheme is national in scope, so its effect on a visitor to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands mirrors what a trans person faces on the mainland: recognition confined to traditional socio-cultural categories and intersex people, with self-identification outside those categories unsupported.

Document and checkpoint friction has been recorded at airports, railway stations and passport offices across India rather than in the islands themselves. The Chennai airport stop of Sakshi Jain in November 2024 and the February 2026 Allahabad High Court relief on passport medical exams indicate that identity verification settings, including those a traveller would meet on arrival or departure, remain a plausible site of scrutiny.

Welfare and healthcare provision varies sharply between Indian states: Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate transgender welfare boards with housing subsidies, pensions and free surgery in public hospitals, while the Ayushman Bharat expansion in April 2024 supplies a national floor for transition-related care. A visitor should not assume mainland state-level benefits travel to the islands.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands fall under the amended Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) framework as it applies across India, with legal recognition routed through medical certification and district-authority processes rather than self-declaration.

The 2021 Madras High Court guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, the 2022 National Medical Commission ban on conversion therapy, and the April 2024 Ayushman Bharat expansion for transition-related healthcare are national instruments that residents can invoke, though implementation outside major mainland centres is uneven.

The August 2024 Ministry of Finance clarification that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on joint bank accounts or partner beneficiary designations applies to residents' financial arrangements.
outOfScopeNotes:
No territory-specific trans law, enforcement record or incident pattern for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands is on file; the assessment rests on the national framework and mainland incident data, and territory-level policing practice remains unresolved.

The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing; whether it has since been assented to and brought into force is unresolved here.

Whether the Ayushman Bharat expansion of April 2024 is fully operational in the islands' healthcare facilities is not sourced.

Reports of clandestine conversion-therapy networks continuing despite the 2021 and 2022 bans give no indication of their presence in the islands; that question is unresolved.
